newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Satirists lighten mood of Bulgarian presidency race.
newsitem.headline: Satirists lighten mood of Bulgarian presidency race.

text.p: Two Bulgarian comedians running a satirical campaign for the presidency against the country's established politicians say they have struck such a chord with disgruntled voters they are now afraid they may even win.

"We think that every intelligent Bulgarian with a sense of humour will support us," said writer and satirist Hristo Boichev. "If people's reaction on the street is anything to go by, we're going to win."

Campaigning for the October 27 election is overshadowed by deep economic crisis and by the October 2 killing of former prime minister Andrei Lukanov, a millionaire businessman and parliamentary deputy for the ruling Socialists.
Bulgaria's 8.5 million people are most concerned at monthly inflation averaging nearly 20 percent and the prospect of power cuts and bread shortages during the approaching Balkan winter.

The national currency has collapsed from 70 lev to the dollar in January to around 215 now. The International Monetary Fund has delayed the badly-needed $115 million second tranche of a standby facility because of the slow pace of economic reform.

"Our aim is not exactly to win the elections but to protest against the political forces that created the economic situation," Boichev's colleague and fellow candidate Ivan Koulekov told Reuters in an interview on Wednesday.
He said they had decided to run on a joint ticket to introduce some much-needed irony into proceedings.

"Our campaign can be looked on as a form of political theatre with the participation of the whole Bulgarian people," he said. "Bulgarians have a very strong social sense of humour and we will give them the opportunity to express it."
A Socialist colleague of the murdwered Lukanov, Andrei Raichev, said last week the controversial former premier had been about to expose high-level government corruption when he was killed.
President Zhelyu Zhelev, meeting foreign ambassadors on Tuesday, told them the killing would not affect the elections.

Boichev, 46, and Koulekov, 45, tried to run for president and vice-president in January 1992 but were rejected on a technicality. This time they are backed by a small party called the Movement of Pensioners, the Jobless and the Poor.
"Most candidates campaign around the country just to get on television for a minute and a half. We can do this without going around the country," Koulekov said.
One of their recent television spots contained a minute's silence to mourn Bulgaria's crisis.

Daily stunts are faithfully reported by state media. On Wednesday, the duo visited a prominent Armenian cleric -- "complaining to the Armenian priest" is a Bulgarian expression for uselessly lamenting one's problems.

Boichev said they planned to meet animals in Sofia zoo and also some of the city's roaming hordes of stray dogs. "We could give them condoms, it might solve the problem," Koulekov said of a population boom which Sofia council is trying to resolve.

Zhelev lost a U.S.-style party primary in June and is not seeking re-election. His Union of Democratic Forces has put up lawyer Petar Stoyanov against Culture Minister Ivan Marazov, the candidate of the Bulgarian Socialist Party.

The Central Electoral Committee has registered 13 candidacies. If no one wins an outright majority, a second round will be held a week later, and Boichev and Koulekov promise to keep up their artistic backing throughout.
"The sense of humour is the one thing that sustains Bulgarians and I think it's the sense of humour that dies last, not hope," Koulekov said.
